questions.problem:
Consider a linear transformation $T$ that maps ${R}^{2}$ to the origin. Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\text{rank}(T)=1$,  where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$

II. $\text{Im}(T)$ contains no vectors of ${R}^{2}$

III. $\text{Ker}(T)={R}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is the zero-subspace $\{0\},$ then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=0
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. In our case, we have 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=0.
$$

- Statement II is false. The image of $T$ contains the vector zero vector $0=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the condition $\text{nullity}(T)=2$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)={R}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem:
If $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto the line $y=-3x$ then, which of the following statements are true?

I. $⟨1,3⟩$ belongs to the range of $T$

II. $\text{Ker}(T)\ne \{0\}$

III. $\text{Im}(T)=\{0\}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is a one-dimensional line, then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=1
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn. 

- Statement I is false. 
Notice that the point $(1,3)$ does not satisfy the equation of the line $y=-3x$ since $3\ne -3\cdot 1.$ Therefore, the vector $⟨1,3⟩\notin \text{Im}(T).$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, 
since $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line passing through the origin, we have that the standard matrix $T$ is singular. Hence, $\text{Ker}(T)\ne \{0\}.$

- Statement III is false. 
For example,  the point $(1,-3)$ satisfies the equation  $y=-3x$ since $-3=-3\cdot 1.$ Therefore, the vector $⟨1,-3⟩\in \text{Im}(T).$ Thus, $\text{Im}(T)\ne \{0\}.$

Let
$T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$
be the standard matrix of the linear transformation $T.$ Then $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $T$ has proportional rows, and yet $T$ is not the zero matrix. 

Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=1$ and $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line that passes through the origin.

Moreover, the line must pass through the origin $(0,0)$ and the points $(1,-1)$ and $(-1,1),$ which are defined by the columns of the matrix $T.$ 

Computing the slope $m$ of this line, we get

$$
m=\frac{1-(-1)}{-1-1}=-1.
$$

 

Therefore, $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto the line $y=-x.$

questions.problem:
Consider a linear transformation $T$ that maps ${R}^{2}$ onto the line $y=2x.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $⟨2,1⟩\in \text{Im}(T)$

II. $\text{Ker}(T)\ne \{0\}$

III. $\text{nullity}(T)=2$, where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is a one-dimensional line, then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=1,
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. The point $(2,1)$ does not satisfy the equation of the line $y=2x$ since $1\ne 2\cdot 2.$ Hence, 

$$
⟨2,1⟩\notin \text{Im}(T).
$$

- Statement II is true. Since $\text{nullity}(T)=1,$ we get 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)\ne \{0\}.
$$

- Statement III is false. We have that 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."
